title: Building Actions
summary: Write functions with multiple steps inside them — and see how the order of lines matters.

content.title: Multiple Lines Inside a Function
content.summary: Every indented line inside the function runs in order, top to bottom, each time you call it.
content.body:
A function can do as many things as you like. Every indented line is part of it:

def open_treasure():
    print("The chest creaks open...")
    print("A golden light spills out.")
    print("You found 50 gold!")

open_treasure()

Python runs all three print lines in order, every time you call open_treasure().

content.title: Order Matters
content.summary: Lines inside a function run top to bottom, just like normal code — sequence is everything.
content.body:
The lines inside a function run in the exact order you write them:

def enter_shop():
    print("A bell jingles as you enter.")
    print("The shopkeeper looks up.")
    print("What would you like to buy?")

If you swapped the last two lines, the shopkeeper would speak before looking up. Order tells the story.

content.title: Where Does the Function End?
content.summary: The function ends when indentation goes back to the left margin.
content.body:
Python knows the function is finished when the indent stops:

def battle():
    print("The enemy charges!")   <- inside the function
    print("You dodge!")            <- inside the function

print("Battle over.")             <- outside the function (no indent)

The last print runs once, after any calls to battle().

content.title: Using Variables Inside Functions
content.summary: You can use variables inside a function body just like anywhere else.
content.body:
Functions can use variables defined inside them:

def show_score():
    score = 100
    print("Current score:", score)

show_score()

The variable score exists while the function runs. Each call to show_score() starts fresh.

editorPrompt: Write a function called open_treasure() with at least 3 print lines describing finding treasure. Then write a function called game_over() with 2 lines. Call them both.
progressiveHints: Replace each `pass` with 2–3 indented print() lines describing that moment.
Make sure every line inside the function is indented 4 spaces.
After both definitions, write open_treasure() and game_over() to call them.

Answer shape:
def open_treasure():
    print("You found a chest!")
    print("Inside: a magic sword.")

def game_over():
    print("Game over.")
    print("Thanks for playing!")

open_treasure()
game_over()
challenge: Add a third function called level_up() that prints a short celebration. Now call them in this order: open_treasure(), level_up(), game_over().
